title: Europe faces faster cyberattacks than ever. But many of the solutions are long known
gist: Chatham House argues Europe's cyber threat is defined by speed, not novelty: the October 2026 hack of refrigeration controllers in ~700 French supermarkets (blamed by France on Iran) exploited unpatched legacy OT, and ENISA says two-thirds of exploited vulnerabilities already have patches. AI is compressing attack timelines rather than creating new attack classes, while Europe's response lags on implementation — all but two member states missed the NIS2 deadline, the EU AI alert system stalled, and defensive AI depends on US tools exposed to export controls.

insights.claim: Europe's cyber exposure can be decomposed into four distinct problems, each needing its own response: unpatched legacy systems, new technology built without security, AI-aided attackers, and states using cyberattacks (often via proxies) as instruments of power.

insights.so_what: Low-sophistication attacks on unpatched OT can cause large physical losses — the attack cost/damage asymmetry favours attackers.

insights.claim: Operational technology that controls physical equipment often stays in service for decades, long after anyone is updating it, creating a growing stock of known, exploitable vulnerabilities.

insights.claim: Public sector IT is itself badly outdated: the UK National Audit Office found in 2025 that departments used 'hundreds of ageing legacy IT systems', and Germany's federal audit office found parts of federal networks so outdated they no longer receive security updates.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Government IT modernisation in the UK and Germany is a sizeable, audit-backed backlog likely to drive public procurement.

insights.claim: Europe does not lack information or rules — it has ENISA's European Vulnerability Database, national alerts and the NIS2 Directive — the missing piece is implementation, especially in smaller organizations, and enforcement in slow-adopting member states.

insights.claim: From December 2027, the EU Cyber Resilience Act will bar connected products that fail basic security requirements from the EU market and make manufacturers responsible for security across the product lifecycle.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A hard compliance date for connected-device makers selling in the EU — raises costs for low-end IoT vendors and may favour scaled, compliant players.

insights.claim: The Cyber Resilience Act has limits: it requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities, but reporting a flaw does not fix it, and for unsupported products there may be no fix, leaving shops, hospitals or councils to patch, isolate or replace equipment themselves.

insights.claim: The underlying problem is poor-quality software; AI could strengthen security by finding and fixing flaws faster than people, but only if vendors use AI tools with human oversight before products reach the market.

insights.so_what: Pre-release AI code-security tooling is the defensive use case with the most leverage.

insights.claim: AI is accelerating how quickly attackers find and exploit vulnerabilities in insecure products and ageing systems, lowering the skills and resources needed and compressing defenders' response time.

insights.claim: The real change in Europe's cyber threat is the timescale, not the type: known weaknesses, insecure products, more capable attackers and fragmented responses; Europe must secure or replace legacy tech, enforce secure-by-design, use AI for defence, and build capacity to disrupt attackers and impose deterring costs.
